Lessons.Title: Design Your Own Robot
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 original IM Grade 3 Unit 7 Lesson 15 teacher lesson and preparation, three-page student PDF and the original Square Dot Paper Standard blackline master were reviewed from the connected device. The source contains a single major student creation activity, not a set of compulsory unique scalar answers. Source publisher art and gated assessment are not embedded.

Warm-up What Do You Know About Area and Perimeter? requires learners to explain the contrast between linear boundary length and square-unit surface and describe calculating strategies. It is a 10-minute teacher-led conversation, not a true-false or fixed-score prompt.

Original 15.1 robot specifications: create the head as a rectangle of PERIMETER 36 units; neck perimeter 8; body perimeter 64; EACH of two arms perimeter 24; EACH of two legs perimeter 32; and ONE additional rectangular feature chosen by the student. Every part must be a rectangle, and students must justify the dimensions they draw.

The original activity also asks pupils to calculate AREA of EACH drawn robot part and TOTAL area of their particular robot, then discuss at a Gallery Walk why distinct rectangles with matching perimeter can have different areas. None of these perimeters alone determines a unique area, so there is no universal numeric correct total area to invent. For a rectangle with fixed perimeter P, a+b=P/2 and area ab can vary.

For illustration, a head with dimensions 8 by 10 has perimeter 36 and area 80 square units; another 6 by 12 head also perimeter 36 has area 72. Neck 1 by 3 gives perimeter 8 and area 3, while 2 by 2 also perimeter 8 has area 4. Such examples are independently created to teach choices, NOT the one mandated publisher drawing or total area.

Source preparation explicitly requires at least TWO sheets of standard square dot paper taped together for the whole robot, plus tape and optional colouring. Teacher supervises rectangular closure, all seven mandatory anatomical parts plus optional feature, perimeters and per-part total area, and gallery discussions with roles exchanged. The 35-minute original Activity 1 follows 10-minute warm-up and precedes 10-minute synthesis and five-minute gated Cool-down.

Original lesson synthesis asks pupils what other real-world objects (such as architecture or vehicles) they might design using shapes, perimeter and area. The original publisher restricted Cool-down Reflect on Learning About Perimeter remains unaccessed, and new first-party practice is not that assessment. No executable tests, CI, Stage D, academic signoff or published Rich V2 confirmation was performed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Source mathematics
KeyConcepts.Definition: Apply the mathematical quantities required by the original activity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Preserve the source units, diagrams and teacher review boundary.
KeyConcepts.Example: Both 8×10 and 6×12 head designs have perimeter36 but unequal areas 80 and 72.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed rectangle perimeter does not fix area
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rectangle with perimeter P has side lengths adding to P/2, but its area changes with the factor pair.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use 2 × (length + width) = P for each robot part, then compute its own length × width area.
KeyConcepts.Example: A head with perimeter 36 can be 8×10 (area 80) or 6×12 (area 72) square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Total area is specific to the student's complete drawn robot
KeyConcepts.Definition: The sum of the areas of all actual nonoverlapping rectangles, including the chosen feature, depends on the student's design.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Verify each part's prescribed perimeter and sum its actual square-unit areas; physical drawing and gallery explanation remain teacher-reviewed.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 1×3 neck and a 2×2 neck both have perimeter 8 but add 3 or 4 square units respectively.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mathematical example
WorkedExamples.Question: Give two rectangles for a head whose source perimeter is 36 units.
WorkedExamples.Method: For rectangle perimeter P, dimensions must add to 18.
Steps: 8+10=18 and 2×18=36; its area is80 square units.
6+12=18 and 2×18=36; its area is72 square units.
Teacher inspects each entire robot and its total area.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 8×10 and 6×12 are two permissible head designs with different areas.
WorkedExamples.Check: This example does not certify original open visuals or discussions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent robot neck dimension choices
WorkedExamples.Question: Find two different rectangles with perimeter 8 units and compare their areas.
WorkedExamples.Method: For a fixed rectangular perimeter 8, side lengths sum to 4.
Steps: Choose lengths 1 and 3, sum 4, perimeter 8, area 3.
Choose lengths 2 and 2, sum 4, perimeter 8, area 4.
Both satisfy the same perimeter but have different areas.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 1×3 gives area 3; 2×2 gives area 4 square units.
WorkedExamples.Check: These are independent permissible examples, not a source-mandated robot drawing.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent rectangle arm calculation
WorkedExamples.Question: For an arm with source-required perimeter 24, does a rectangle 5 by 7 meet the perimeter constraint, and what is its area?
WorkedExamples.Method: Check fixed perimeter and calculate area separately.
Steps: Teacher checks that each of the two student-created arms independently meets the source perimeter and that total robot area is from the actual drawing.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes; 35 square units for this arm.
WorkedExamples.Check: Not the universal robot's area and not a replacement for pupil construction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Grade an original open task from a single number.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original source requires modelling, visuals or explanation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the original materials and seek teacher review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Concluding that rectangles with the same perimeter must have equal areas.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: For a fixed perimeter, multiple length–width pairs have the same sum but can have different products.
CommonMistakes.Correction: For each actual robot rectangle, check 2 × (length + width) against the required perimeter, then calculate length × width separately.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up is open area-versus-perimeter teaching conversation.
Source robot requirements: head P36, neck P8, body P64, each arm P24, each leg P32 plus an extra rectangular feature.
Compute area of every chosen part and YOUR complete robot; there is no single universal total area.
At least two original dot-grid sheets taped together for robot; teacher-led gallery walk.
Publisher original reflective Cool-down is gated; Stage D/CI not run.
